overview.bigIdea: Two countries, two choices. **Belgium shared power and stayed united; Sri Lanka imposed the majority’s will and fell into civil war.** From these stories we learn *why* democracies share power and the four *ways* they do it.

ladder.a: Belgium accommodated; Sri Lanka followed majoritarianism

lessons.title: Belgium and Sri Lanka
lessons.hook: Imagine a country where most people speak one language, but the rich and powerful capital city speaks another. Belgium faced exactly this – and chose to **share** power. Sri Lanka, with an even bigger majority, chose to **dominate**. Their results could not be more different.

core.def: 59% Dutch-speaking (Flemish region), 40% French-speaking (Wallonia), 1% German. In Brussels: 80% French, 20% Dutch.

Sinhala-speakers 74%, Tamil-speakers 18% (Sri Lankan Tamils 13% in north and east; Indian Tamils – plantation workers’ descendants). Most Sinhalas are Buddhist; most Tamils Hindu or Muslim; about 7% Christians.
Belief that the majority community should rule in whichever way it wants, disregarding the wishes and needs of the minority.
1956 Act: Sinhala the only official language · preference to Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs · constitution to protect and foster Buddhism.

Equal Dutch and French ministers at the Centre · state governments not subordinate · Brussels government with equal representation · community government for cultural, educational and language issues.

explain: **Sri Lanka:** independent in 1948. Majoritarian measures made Sri Lankan Tamils feel alienated. They demanded Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy and equal opportunity; by the 1980s groups demanded an independent Tamil Eelam. Distrust turned into a civil war that ended in 2009.

**Belgium:** between 1970 and 1993 it amended its constitution four times. The arrangement is complicated, but it avoided civic strife and a possible division on linguistic lines – Brussels even became the headquarters of the European Union.

example.q: Describe the elements of the Belgian model of power sharing. (5 marks)
steps: **Equal ministers:** the constitution prescribes an equal number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers in the central government; some laws need a majority from each linguistic group.
**State governments:** many powers of the central government were given to the state governments of the two regions, which are not subordinate to the Centre.
**Brussels:** has a separate government in which both communities have equal representation.
**Community government:** a third kind of government, elected by each language community (Dutch, French, German) wherever they live, with power over cultural, educational and language-related issues.
**Result:** civic strife and a division of the country on linguistic lines were avoided.
example.answer: Five points: equal ministers, powerful states, Brussels, community government, result.

mistakes: Mixing up the percentages – Dutch are the majority in Belgium but the minority in Brussels.
Writing that Belgium is a unitary state – it became federal in 1993.
Forgetting to say WHAT the community government deals with (culture, education, language).
lessons.tip: For ‘Compare Belgium and Sri Lanka’ questions, draw a two-column table: Composition · Policy · Result.

lessons.title: Why power sharing is desirable
lessons.hook: Is sharing power the same as weakening a country? Belgium says no: sharing made it **stronger and more united**. There are two kinds of reasons – one practical, one about values.

core.def: Based on careful calculation of gains and losses. Power sharing reduces conflict between social groups and ensures political stability.
Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy: people have a right to be consulted on how they are governed.
One where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system.
Oppressive for the minority and often harmful for the majority too; it undermines national unity in the long run.

explain: Prudential reasons stress that power sharing brings **better outcomes**; moral reasons emphasise the **act** of sharing as valuable in itself.
Indian example: reserving seats in panchayats for women and SC/ST reduces feelings of exclusion (prudential) and gives them a voice in decisions that affect them (moral).

example.q: State one prudential and one moral reason for power sharing, with an Indian example. (3 marks)
steps: **Prudential:** power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups and ensures stability – e.g. forming linguistic states in India reduced tension and made the country more united.
**Moral:** it is the spirit of democracy – people affected by decisions must be consulted – e.g. gram sabhas let villagers approve their panchayat’s budget.
Conclusion: both reasons support sharing power in a diverse country like India.
example.answer: One prudential + one moral reason, each with an example.

mistakes: Swapping the two types of reasons.
Giving reasons without examples when the question asks for them.
Saying power sharing always slows a country down – the chapter argues it strengthens unity.
lessons.tip: Memorise the two opening lines: ‘Prudential reasons stress better outcomes’ and ‘Moral reasons value the act of sharing itself’.
lessons.memory: Prudential = Practical results. Moral = Meaning of democracy.

lessons.title: Forms of power sharing
lessons.hook: In a democracy, people are the source of all political power. So power is not kept in one place – it is spread out in **four different ways**. Spotting which way is being used in a news story is a favourite exam question.

core.def: Legislature, executive and judiciary at the same level exercise different powers → checks and balances. E.g. judges can check laws and the executive.
Union/federal government, State governments and local bodies (municipalities, panchayats). Called federal division of power.
Religious and linguistic groups, weaker sections and women. E.g. Belgium’s community government; reserved constituencies in India.

core.term: 4 · Among parties, pressure groups and movements
core.def: Competition among parties; coalitions when parties form alliances; interest groups (traders, farmers, workers) influence decisions.

explain: Horizontal: organs at the **same** level check each other – ministers are responsible to Parliament; judges, though appointed by the executive, can check it.
Vertical: **higher and lower** levels, each with powers laid down in the constitution – done in Belgium, refused in Sri Lanka.

example.q: What are the different forms of power sharing in modern democracies? Give an example of each. (5 marks)
steps: **Horizontal distribution** among legislature, executive and judiciary – e.g. the judiciary can strike down laws made by the legislature (checks and balances).
**Vertical division** among levels of government – e.g. Union Government, State Governments and panchayats in India.
**Among social groups** – e.g. community government in Belgium; reserved constituencies for SC/ST in India.
**Among political parties, pressure groups and movements** – e.g. coalition governments; farmers’ and traders’ groups influencing policies.
Such arrangements ensure that power does not remain in one hand.
example.answer: Four forms, each with an example, plus a concluding line.

mistakes: Forgetting pressure groups and movements in the fourth form.
Giving only foreign examples when an Indian example is asked.
lessons.tip: Remember the order O-L-S-P: Organs, Levels, Social groups, Parties. Each gets one example.
lessons.memory: Organs side-by-side = horizontal. Levels up-and-down = vertical.

revision: Belgium: 59% Dutch (Flemish), 40% French (Wallonia), 1% German; Brussels 80% French, 20% Dutch.
Sri Lanka: independent 1948; Sinhala 74%, Tamil 18% (Sri Lankan Tamils 13%, rest Indian Tamils).
Majoritarian measures: 1956 Sinhala-only Act; preference for Sinhala in universities and jobs; state to protect and foster Buddhism.
Result in Sri Lanka: Tamil alienation → demand for Tamil Eelam (1980s) → civil war, ended 2009.
Belgian model (1970–1993): equal ministers; states not subordinate; Brussels equal representation; community government.
Lesson: Belgium’s unity came from respecting diversity; Sri Lanka shows majority domination undermines unity.
Prudential reasons: reduce conflict, ensure stability. Moral reasons: spirit of democracy, right to be consulted, legitimacy.
Four forms: organs (horizontal, checks and balances), levels (vertical, federal), social groups, parties/pressure groups/movements.
Lebanon pact: President Maronite Christian, PM Sunni, Deputy PM Orthodox Christian, Speaker Shi’a.

sections.title: Comparison questions · 4 steps
items: Draw two columns: Belgium | Sri Lanka.
Row 1 composition, Row 2 what the government did, Row 3 result.
Add one number or date in each column (59%, 1956, 1970–93, 2009).
End with the lesson: accommodation strengthens unity; majoritarianism weakens it.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line definition or introduction using textbook keywords (e.g. ‘Majoritarianism is …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, with the key term in the first few words. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a real example from the chapter to each point (Belgium, Sri Lanka, Panchayati Raj, a party, a survey figure).
Use the exact numbers the textbook gives only when you are sure (59%, 1956, 1992, one-third, 1976).
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ questions use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Distinguish’ questions draw a small two-column table.
Case-based questions: underline the key line in the passage first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn sorts – if you can sort every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can give the language composition of Belgium and Sri Lanka.
I can list three majoritarian measures of Sri Lanka and their result.
I can describe four elements of the Belgian model.

I can name the four forms of power sharing and classify any example.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark case/source-based and 5-mark long answers). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
